narrative.text: Opening page of a 2007 Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal article in French on a pilot antiretroviral therapy study in Djibouti, with an abstract describing a survey of 112 HIV-positive patients and their treatment efficacy. The Arabic abstract on this page was extracted as garbled text, and the footer also contains garbled characters.

Introduces the Djibouti antiretroviral therapy study, giving the country's HIV prevalence, treatment eligibility criteria and first- and second-line regimens. It sets out the study objectives and begins describing methods, including how virological efficacy was assessed; the footer is garbled text.

Defines the criteria for virological and immunological success or failure and for blood abnormalities, and describes the laboratory techniques used for CD4 counts, viral load and blood counts. It begins the results with patients' sociodemographic profile; the footer contains garbled text.

Reports where patients in the Djibouti study were followed up and their main opportunistic infections at treatment start, with a table of sociodemographic characteristics. It gives the share of patients achieving virological success and notes that efficacy did not differ by regimen.

Presents a table of the study population's clinical, biological and treatment characteristics and reports significant clinical improvement, such as gains in Karnofsky index and body mass index and fewer opportunistic infections. It ends with a table listing the antiretroviral combinations prescribed.

Gives a table of immunological and virological efficacy and reports a strong correlation between total lymphocytes and CD4 counts, testing different lymphocyte thresholds for starting treatment. It identifies predictors of failure and opens the discussion on low treatment coverage in Djibouti.

Presents a table comparing clinical, immunological, haematological and biochemical parameters at treatment start and at the time of the survey. The discussion begins comparing the sociodemographic profile with African studies.

Shows a regression plot of the correlation between total lymphocytes and CD4 cells at treatment start, with the figure partly extracted as garbled characters. The discussion compares opportunistic infections, HIV-1 predominance and protease inhibitor use with other African countries and explains the clinical improvement seen.
A table from the multivariate logistic regression identifying factors that predict treatment success, including treatment centre, initial Karnofsky index and clinical stage.

Continues the discussion, comparing treatment efficacy with other countries and noting immunological-virological discordance. It discusses the limits of total lymphocyte counts as a CD4 substitute, attributes viral rebound mainly to poor adherence, and notes possible information and classification biases.

Concludes that antiretroviral therapy is feasible and effective in Djibouti but that central structures and care of opportunistic infections should be strengthened before scale-up. Acknowledgements and the start of the reference list follow.
The end of the reference list for the Djibouti antiretroviral therapy article, citing mainly AIDS and JAMA studies on CD4 counts, total lymphocyte counts, drug resistance and adverse effects.
